chapter_title: Introduction to UMG and Widget Blueprints
chapter_summary:
Welcome to the exciting world of User Interface (UI) design in Unreal Engine! For game developers, a well-crafted UI is just as crucial as compelling gameplay. It's the primary way players interact with your game, receive feedback, and navigate through menus. Unreal Engine provides a powerful and flexible system for this called Universal Widget Markup, or UMG. UMG allows you to create UI elements entirely within Blueprints, making it accessible even without extensive C++ knowledge. Think of UMG as your digital canvas for building everything from health bars and ammo counters (Heads-Up Display or HUD) to intricate main menus, inventory screens, and quest logs. It's a declarative UI system, meaning you describe what your UI should look like, and UMG handles the rendering.

To begin our journey with UMG, let's create our very first Widget Blueprint. In the Content Browser, right-click, navigate to "User Interface," and select "Widget Blueprint." When prompted, choose `UserWidget` as the parent class. This `UserWidget` class is the foundation for all custom UI elements you'll create. Name your new widget something descriptive, like `WBP_PlayerHUD`. Double-clicking this asset opens the Widget Blueprint Editor, which is divided into two main tabs: Designer and Graph. The Designer tab is where you visually construct your UI using a drag-and-drop interface, while the Graph tab is where you add the Blueprint logic to make your UI interactive.

In the Designer tab, you'll find a Palette panel on the left containing various UI elements, known as "widgets." Let's start with some basics. Drag a `TextBlock` from the Palette onto the Canvas Panel in the middle. The Canvas Panel is a flexible layout container that allows you to position widgets using absolute coordinates or anchors. Once you've placed the `TextBlock`, select it and look at the Details panel on the right. Here, you can modify its properties. Change the "Text" property to something like "Player Health: 100". You can also adjust its font, size, color, and position. Next, let's add a `Button`. Drag a `Button` widget from the Palette onto the Canvas Panel. Position it below your `TextBlock`. A common mistake here is not giving your button any visual feedback. By default, a button is just a transparent rectangle. To make it visible, you can either drag a `TextBlock` *onto* the button to serve as its label, or you can set its "Style" properties to include an image or color. For simplicity, drag a `TextBlock` onto the `Button` and change its text to "Heal Player". Notice how the `TextBlock` automatically becomes a child of the `Button`, ensuring it moves and scales with it.

Now that we've designed a basic HUD, the next crucial step is to display it on the player's screen. Widgets don't automatically appear; they need to be explicitly created and added to the viewport. The best place to do this for a persistent HUD is typically within the `PlayerController` or the `GameMode`, as these Blueprints persist across level changes or manage game state. For a quick test, we can do this in the `Level Blueprint`. Open your current level's Blueprint (Blueprints -> Open Level Blueprint). From the `Event BeginPlay` node, drag off an execution pin and search for `Create Widget`. For the "Widget Class" pin, select your `WBP_PlayerHUD`. This node creates an instance of your widget. The return value from `Create Widget` is a reference to the newly created widget. From this return value, drag off and search for `Add to Viewport`. This node takes the widget instance and renders it on the screen. Connect the execution pins, compile, and save. When you play your game, you should now see your "Player Health" text and "Heal Player" button on the screen.

A common mistake beginners make is creating the widget but forgetting to `Add to Viewport`, resulting in the UI not appearing. Another frequent issue is trying to access widget elements (like a `TextBlock` or `Button`) from other Blueprints *before* the widget has been created and added to the viewport. Always ensure the widget's lifecycle is correctly managed. Furthermore, remember that the `Canvas Panel` is very flexible but can be tricky for responsive UI across different screen resolutions. While we used it for simple positioning, for more complex layouts that need to adapt, we'll explore other layout panels in later chapters. For now, focus on understanding the fundamental flow: create the Widget Blueprint, design it in the Designer tab, and then create an instance and add it to the viewport from a suitable gameplay Blueprint. This foundational understanding is key to building any interactive UI in Unreal Engine.

screens.title: Introduction to UMG and Widget Blueprints
screens.subtitle: Build playable HUDs and menus in Blueprints without writing C++

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you'll learn how Unreal's UMG system turns visual layouts into interactive UI using Widget Blueprints. UMG, sometimes called Unreal Motion Graphics, is the engine's visual UI toolkit that lets you design elements like health bars, score displays, and menus entirely inside Blueprints. You'll see how to create a Widget Blueprint asset, use the Designer tab to place widgets such as TextBlock and Button, and add simple Blueprint logic in the Graph tab. We'll also walk through the runtime steps required so your widget actually appears on screen: creating an instance with the Create Widget node and rendering it with Add to Viewport. This matters because UI is how players receive feedback and control the game. A missing Add to Viewport or mismanaged widget lifecycle is a common reason UIs fail to show or update. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to make a basic HUD, understand where to construct persistent widgets, and spot common setup mistakes. Think of this as the foundation for all HUD and menu work; once you can reliably display widgets, you can iterate on layout, binding, and interactivity.

keyIdea.text: UMG + Widget Blueprints let you design and run UI visually in Blueprints; create the widget asset, design it, then instantiate and add it to the viewport at runtime.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: In this chapter you will gain four practical skills that let you design and display working UI in Unreal without C++. First, you'll understand the role of UMG as the visual UI system for in-game interfaces and menus. This means being able to explain why UMG belongs in the asset workflow and how it fits the Designer and Graph workflow. Second, you'll create a Widget Blueprint and add core widgets like TextBlock and Button, including adjusting properties such as text, font size, and color. Third, you'll learn how to arrange UI using basic panels, especially the Canvas Panel with anchors and absolute placement, and why anchors matter for different screen sizes. Fourth, you'll wire up runtime display using Create Widget and Add to Viewport from an appropriate Blueprint. Each objective includes a short example and a small mnemonic to help you remember the flow from asset to screen. By the end you'll also be able to identify common beginner mistakes so you can debug why a widget doesn't appear or why its children are inaccessible.

screens.title: How you'll practice these skills
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step design, runtime wiring, and common debugging checks

narration.text: This second objectives slide focuses on practice: you'll build, test, and debug a simple HUD. The practice workflow begins by creating a Widget Blueprint asset named descriptively, for example WBP_ScoreHUD, and opening it in the Designer. There you'll place a TextBlock for Score and optionally another for High Score. Next, anchor and position these elements so they remain visible across resolutions. Then open a gameplay Blueprint — the Level Blueprint for a quick test, or PlayerController/GameMode for persistent UI — and from Event BeginPlay call Create Widget and choose your WBP_ScoreHUD. Immediately follow that with Add to Viewport so the instance renders. Finally, test play and observe if the widget appears. If it doesn't, check that Add to Viewport was called and that Visibility isn't set to Hidden. Also ensure you aren't referencing widget children before the widget is created. This practice loop teaches you the lifecycle: asset creation, visual design, instantiate at runtime, confirm, and debug.

screens.title: What is UMG (Unreal Motion Graphics)?
screens.subtitle: A visual UI system for Blueprints and in-game interfaces

narration.text: UMG, or Unreal Motion Graphics, is the visual UI framework built into Unreal Engine that allows you to design interactive interfaces without writing C++. It's a declarative system where you assemble widgets—small UI building blocks—inside a Widget Blueprint asset and define interaction logic in the same asset's Graph. UMG matters because it separates visual layout from gameplay logic: designers can craft HUDs and menus visually while programmers or scripters attach behavior in Blueprints. A simple example is a health display: a TextBlock shows the numeric health while a ProgressBar can reflect percentage. Those widgets live inside a UserWidget subclass which stores both appearance and event handling. A common misconception is that UMG is only for static menus; in reality UMG supports dynamic runtime updates, event bindings, and complex interactions through Blueprint nodes. Another confusion is thinking a Widget Blueprint automatically appears—creating the asset is not enough; you must instantiate it at runtime and add it to the viewport. The key takeaway is that UMG provides both the canvas and the wiring for UI: asset creation, visual design, and Blueprint logic together let you produce fully interactive interfaces.

keyIdea.title: UMG definition
keyIdea.text: UMG is Unreal's visual UI framework that combines Designer layout and Blueprint logic in Widget Blueprints.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › What is UMG?
Definition & Role
UMG is the visual UI system in Unreal used to create HUDs, menus, and interactive overlays.
Designer + Graph
Designer: layout; Graph: event handling and bindings.
UserWidget
Base class for custom widgets that holds visuals and logic.
Runtime lifecycle
Create an instance, then Add to Viewport to render it.
Concrete example
Imagine a Player Health display: a TextBlock shows current health while a ProgressBar fills to the health percentage. You create the widget asset, place those widgets in the Designer, and in the Graph bind a function that updates the TextBlock whenever health changes.
Misconception
Creating the asset alone does not display it. You must instantiate and add it to the viewport.
Why it matters
UI delivers player feedback and controls; good UMG design improves usability and accessibility of your game.
Key Takeaway

UMG combines visual layout and Blueprint logic to produce interactive UI. Asset creation, visual design, and runtime instantiation form the complete UMG workflow.

screens.title: Creating a Widget Blueprint
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step to make your first UserWidget asset

narration.text: Let's walk through creating a Widget Blueprint so you can start building UI immediately. First, in the Content Browser right-click, choose User Interface and pick Widget Blueprint. When prompted choose UserWidget as the parent class — that establishes the base behavior for your UI asset. Name the asset something descriptive like WBP_PlayerHUD or WBP_ScoreHUD so its purpose is clear. Double-click the new asset to open the Widget Blueprint Editor. Notice the Designer tab for visual layout and the Graph tab for logic. In Designer you'll see a Palette of widgets such as TextBlock, Button, Image and containers like Canvas Panel. Drag a TextBlock onto the Canvas Panel and set its Text property to a sample value like Player Health: 100. Then drag a Button and drop a TextBlock onto the Button to label it, for example Heal Player. Save your widget asset. This process creates an editable blueprint that contains both the visual tree and event graph you will later instantiate at runtime. A common slip is naming assets generically; use clear names so other team members and Blueprints can reference them easily.

keyIdea.title: Create workflow
keyIdea.text: Right-click Content Browser → User Interface → Widget Blueprint; open it and design in Designer, then add logic in Graph.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Creating a Widget Blueprint
Step-by-step
Create and name a UserWidget asset, then design basic elements.
1. Create asset
Right-click Content Browser → User Interface → Widget Blueprint. Choose UserWidget.
2. Name it clearly
Use WBP_PlayerHUD or WBP_ScoreHUD so purpose is obvious to other designers.
3. Open Designer
Drag TextBlock, Button, Image, and containers from the Palette.
4. Save and test
Save the asset before instantiating at runtime to avoid stale references.
Concrete example
Create WBP_PlayerHUD, add a TextBlock with text "Player Health: 100", then a Button labeled "Heal Player". Nest the TextBlock inside the Button to ensure it moves with the button.
Key Takeaway

A Widget Blueprint is both visual and logical. Name assets clearly and save before runtime use.

screens.title: Designer Tab vs Graph Tab
screens.subtitle: Where you build visuals and where you add interactivity

narration.text: Understanding the Designer and Graph tabs is essential for productive UMG work. The Designer tab is a visual canvas. You drag widgets from the Palette, place them into containers like Canvas Panel, and configure appearance properties such as text, font, color, and anchors. Designer is the place to set the look and static layout of your UI. The Graph tab is where you add Blueprint logic: event handlers, bindings, and functions that change widget state at runtime. For example, if you want the Heal Player button to increase health, you'll create an OnClicked event in the Graph and connect it to a function or event on the player that modifies health and updates the TextBlock. A frequent misconception is that the Graph can’t access Designer children; in reality you can expose named widgets as variables and manipulate them in the Graph, but only after the widget has been created and initialized. Another pitfall is relying purely on Designer for dynamic behavior; visuals often need Graph logic to update every frame or in response to gameplay events. The practical rule: Designer for visuals and positioning; Graph for behavior and runtime updates.

keyIdea.title: Division of responsibility
keyIdea.text: Designer defines visuals and layout; Graph handles events and runtime updates that make UI interactive.

content.html:

Designer tab
Visual canvas for layout. Place TextBlock, Button, Image and containers. Set anchors and absolute positions for Canvas Panel.
Drag-and-drop widgets
Adjust properties in Details panel
Set anchors for responsiveness
Graph tab
Add event handlers, bind functions, and update widget children at runtime using Blueprint nodes.
OnClicked and event nodes
Expose widget children as variables
Update TextBlock or ProgressBar dynamically
Example workflow
Place a TextBlock in Designer, give it a name like ScoreText, then in Graph on an event update ScoreText's text when the player earns points. Remember you must create and add the widget instance before Graph updates will take effect in Play mode.
Key Takeaway

Use Designer for structure and Graph for behavior. Name widget children you intend to control in the Graph and ensure the widget instance exists when calling those nodes.

screens.title: Key Widgets: TextBlock and Button
screens.subtitle: How to display text and capture simple clicks

narration.text: Two of the most commonly used UMG widgets are TextBlock and Button. A TextBlock displays static or dynamic text and is ideal for numbers like score or a string such as Player Health: 100. It is lightweight and easy to update from the Graph by exposing it as a variable and setting its text property. A Button is an interactive widget representing a clickable area. By itself a Button may be visually transparent; common practice is to place a TextBlock as a child of the Button to provide a visible label. To react to clicks, use the OnClicked event in the Graph and wire it to gameplay logic, such as calling a Heal function on the player. Beginners often forget to add visible content to a Button, which makes it appear invisible in Designer and Play. Another subtle point is to ensure TextBlock font size and color are legible across resolutions — anchors and font choices both affect readability. Practice by adding a TextBlock inside a Button and creating an OnClicked handler that increases a score variable to see the update in Play mode.

keyIdea.title: TextBlock & Button
keyIdea.text: TextBlock shows text; Button is clickable. Nest a TextBlock inside a Button for a visible label and use OnClicked to respond to presses.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › TextBlock & Button
TextBlock
Used to display text such as Score: 0 or Player Health: 100. Update text from the Graph to reflect gameplay state.
Best practices
  • Expose frequently-updated TextBlocks as variables for quick access in Graph.
  • Pick font size and color for readability at target resolutions.
Button
Represents a clickable area. Add a child TextBlock as a label or set Style properties for visible feedback.
Common pitfall
Buttons can be invisible if you don't place visible content. Always add a label or style the button background.
Quick scenario
Place a Button labeled Heal Player. In the Graph use the OnClicked event to call a function on the player that increases health and then update the health TextBlock. This ties the visual to gameplay behavior.

screens.title: Canvas Panel and Layout Basics
screens.subtitle: Absolute placement, anchors, and responsive considerations

narration.text: The Canvas Panel is the most common layout container for simple HUDs because it offers flexible absolute positioning and anchors. Widgets placed on a Canvas Panel can use explicit X and Y coordinates or anchors that tie positions to screen edges and proportions. Anchors matter when supporting multiple resolutions. For example, anchoring a score TextBlock to the top-left corner keeps it in place when the viewport changes size. However, Canvas Panel's absolute nature makes responsive scaling harder for complex layouts; that's why other layout panels exist for lists, grids, and vertical stacks. A practical tip: anchor first, then set position offsets; this reduces surprises when switching aspect ratios. A common error is positioning items visually in Designer without adjusting anchors — the UI will drift on different screen sizes. If your design needs to adapt, combine Canvas Panel for overlay items and containers like Horizontal Box or Scale Box for grouped elements that should resize. The core idea is to choose Canvas Panel for precise overlay placement, but use anchors and complementary panels to maintain responsiveness. Canvas Panel and Layout Basics means use canvas panel for precise control, but set anchors and combine with other panels when you need responsive layouts.. In practical terms, absolute placement, anchors, and responsive considerations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Canvas Panel rule
keyIdea.text: Use Canvas Panel for precise control, but set anchors and combine with other panels when you need responsive layouts.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Canvas Panel & Layout
Canvas Panel basics
Absolute placement with optional anchors to support relative positioning.
Anchors
Set anchors before position offsets to keep widgets consistent across resolutions.
Absolute coordinates
Use X/Y for exact overlay placement, such as center crosshairs or HUD elements.
Complementary panels
Combine with Boxes or Scale Box for layouts that should resize gracefully.
Practical example
Anchor a Score TextBlock to top-left and set offsets X=20, Y=20. Anchor a High Score to top-right so it remains visible on wide screens.
Key Takeaway
Anchor first, position second. Use Canvas Panel for overlays, but prefer container panels for adaptive content.

screens.title: Display a Widget at Runtime
screens.subtitle: Create Widget and Add to Viewport from BeginPlay

narration.text: To make a widget visible in Play, follow a simple runtime flow: create an instance, then add it to the viewport. Commonly this is done from Event BeginPlay in a Blueprint that persists for the desired lifetime of the UI, such as the PlayerController or GameMode. For a quick test you can use the Level Blueprint. The nodes are Create Widget and Add to Viewport. Create Widget requires a Widget Class input — choose your Widget Blueprint like WBP_PlayerHUD. Its return value is the widget instance. Connect that instance to Add to Viewport to render it. Optionally, store the return value in a variable for later updates or to remove it. A frequent mistake is creating a widget but not calling Add to Viewport, which results in no visible UI. Another error is attempting to access child widget components from other Blueprints before creation; always ensure creation completes before calling functions on widget children. Using PlayerController yields persistence across levels, while Level Blueprint is fine for level-specific quick tests. Always test in Play mode and confirm the widget's Visibility is set to Visible.

keyIdea.title: Runtime flow
keyIdea.text: From BeginPlay: Create Widget (class WBP_...) → Add to Viewport → optionally store the instance for later updates or removal.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Create Widget → Add to Viewport
Runtime steps
Instantiate and render a widget during gameplay using Blueprint nodes.
Create Widget
Select the Widget Class (WBP_PlayerHUD). The node returns an instance reference.
Add to Viewport
Pass the returned instance to render it on screen. Store reference if you will update it later.
Where to call
PlayerController or GameMode for persistent UI; Level Blueprint for quick tests.
Blueprint snippet
// In your Level Blueprint
// Event BeginPlay
//      |
//      V
//   Create Widget (Class: WBP_ScoreHUD)
//      |
//      V
//   Add to Viewport (Target: Return Value from Create Widget)
Key Takeaway

Create an instance before updating or referencing widget children, and always Add to Viewport to make the widget visible.

screens.title: Where to Instantiate Widgets: Level Blueprint vs PlayerController vs GameMode
screens.subtitle: Choose the right place for widget lifetime and access

narration.text: Choosing where to create UI instances affects lifetime and access. Level Blueprint is convenient for rapid testing because it runs when a level begins and is easy to edit, but widgets created there will not persist across level transitions. PlayerController is a recommended place for HUDs tied to a player because the controller persists when possessing pawns and often persists across levels, enabling consistent player UI. GameMode can be suitable for UI that is tied to game rules and state, though GameMode exists only on the server in networked contexts, so use PlayerController for client-side HUDs in multiplayer. A concrete example: create a persistent HUD in PlayerController's BeginPlay so the widget persists when the player moves between levels in the same game session. A common misconception is that one place is strictly correct; in practice the right choice depends on desired lifetime and replication model. The key decision is whether the UI should be level-specific or player-global, and whether it needs to be controlled on the server or client side. Where to Instantiate Widgets: Level Blueprint vs PlayerController vs GameMode means use level blueprint for quick tests, playercontroller for persistent player huds, and gamemode for game-rule related ui; pick based on lifetime and networking needs.. In practical terms, choose the right place for widget lifetime and access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Where to create
keyIdea.text: Use Level Blueprint for quick tests, PlayerController for persistent player HUDs, and GameMode for game-rule related UI; pick based on lifetime and networking needs.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Where to Instantiate
Choose based on lifetime
Level Blueprint, PlayerController, and GameMode each have trade-offs for widget lifecycle and access.
Level Blueprint
Easy for quick tests; not persistent across levels.
PlayerController
Good for persistent HUDs tied to the player; accessible client-side.
GameMode
Useful for game-rule UI; note server-only behavior in multiplayer contexts.
Practical guideline

If UI should follow the player across levels, instantiate it in PlayerController. For level-specific debug UI, Level Blueprint is fastest. Consider networking when choosing GameMode.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity — Basic Score HUD
screens.subtitle: Design, instantiate, and verify a simple Score display

narration.text: Let's put the steps together in a hands-on activity that creates a simple Score HUD. First, make a Widget Blueprint named WBP_ScoreHUD. In Designer add a TextBlock and set its text to Score: 0. Anchor it to the top-left and set offsets like X=20, Y=20 so it stays visible. Expose the TextBlock as a variable named ScoreText so you can update it in the Graph. Save the widget. Next open the Level Blueprint for a quick test or PlayerController for persistent UI. From Event BeginPlay add Create Widget and choose WBP_ScoreHUD. Store the returned value in a variable called HUDInstance, then call Add to Viewport with HUDInstance as the target. To update the score at runtime, call SetText on ScoreText through HUDInstance when the player earns points. A common mistake is calling SetText before creating the widget; ensure the instance exists. When you Play, verify Score: 0 appears and incrementing events update the value. This loop teaches the full lifecycle from design to runtime interaction. Hands-on Activity — Basic Score HUD means design wbp_scorehud with a scoretext textblock, create widget at beginplay, add to viewport, and update via the widget instance reference.. In practical terms, design, instantiate, and verify a simple score display. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Create WBP_ScoreHUD and wire it into BeginPlay.

Level Blueprint

Starter Blueprint snippet
// In your Level Blueprint
// Event BeginPlay
//      |
//      V
//   Create Widget (Class: WBP_ScoreHUD) -> HUDInstance

screens.title: Widget Lifecycle and Common Pitfalls
screens.subtitle: Why widgets don't appear or why child references fail

narration.text: Understanding the widget lifecycle helps you avoid the most common pitfalls. A Widget Blueprint is an asset on disk; it becomes a runtime object only after you call Create Widget. Create Widget returns an instance that must be added to the viewport with Add to Viewport in order to render. Failing either step explains the most frequent 'invisible UI' problem. Another issue arises when other Blueprints try to access widget children before the instance exists. For example, calling SetText on a ScoreText before Create Widget runs will fail. To avoid this, create and store the instance in a variable and only call methods after creation. Visibility and layering can also hide widgets — ensure Visibility is Visible and check Z-order if overlapping elements hide it. Finally, Canvas Panel anchoring issues cause unexpected placement on different resolutions. The debugging sequence is: verify Create Widget was called, confirm Add to Viewport executed, check Visibility, and ensure you are referencing an existing instance when updating children. This structured checklist helps you quickly isolate lifecycle errors. Widget Lifecycle and Common Pitfalls means create the widget instance, add to viewport, ensure visibility is visible, and only update children after the instance exists.. In practical terms, why widgets don't appear or why child references fail. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle checklist
keyIdea.text: Create the widget instance, Add to Viewport, ensure Visibility is Visible, and only update children after the instance exists.

Widget lifecycle checklist
Follow these checks when UI does not appear or behave.
Step 1: Was Create Widget called?
Create an instance before anything else.
Step 2: Add to Viewport
Without this, the instance is not rendered.
Step 3: Visibility and Z-order
Ensure set to Visible and not layered behind other elements.
Common developer error
Accessing widget children from another Blueprint before the widget instance exists leads to null references. Always call child updates after storing the Create Widget return value.

narration.text: Let's use short assessment prompts and debugging strategies to deepen your understanding. First question: You created WBP_MainMenu but it doesn't appear. The likely culprit is forgetting Add to Viewport after Create Widget. Check your nodes and ensure the instance is passed to Add to Viewport. Second prompt: Which widget is best for showing numeric text like a score? The TextBlock is designed to display text and is ideal for dynamic numeric values. For debugging, start with a visibility check: set the widget to Visible and test in Play. Then confirm that Create Widget executes by temporarily printing a log or setting a debug text. If child elements are not updating, confirm that you're referencing the instance returned from Create Widget and not the asset itself. Also test anchors by resizing the Play viewport to reproduce placement issues. These steps — verify creation, visibility, instance references, and anchors — give you a repeatable debugging approach. End with this reflective question: after checking Create Widget and Add to Viewport, what is the next place you would look if the UI is still hidden?

After confirming Create Widget and Add to Viewport, check Visibility and whether another widget is occluding your UI. If still hidden, verify your anchors and screen resolution behavior.

narration.text: Let's summarize three core concepts to carry forward. First, UMG is Unreal's visual UI framework; it combines a Designer for visuals and a Graph for behavior, enabling you to create interactive HUDs and menus inside Blueprints. Second, a Widget Blueprint (UserWidget) is the asset container for UI; you design its visual tree and add logic to react to gameplay. Third, the runtime flow requires Create Widget to instantiate the asset and Add to Viewport to render it; forgetting Add to Viewport is the most frequent reason a UI doesn't appear. Keep these three ideas in mind as you build: toolset (UMG), container (Widget Blueprint/UserWidget), and runtime lifecycle (Create → Add). They form a concise mental model for constructing and debugging UMG-based interfaces. narration.text: A closing checklist helps as you work through exercises. First, always name Widget Blueprints clearly so other assets and Blueprints can reference them easily. Second, place visible content inside Buttons or style the button so it provides user feedback; otherwise buttons may appear invisible. Third, use anchors on the Canvas Panel to maintain position across different screen sizes and pick container panels for adaptive layout. These small habits reduce common errors and speed up iteration. When you next create a HUD, ask: is this widget persistent? If yes, consider PlayerController. Will it be level-only? Level Blueprint is fine for the quick iteration. Finally, when debugging remember the Create Widget and Add to Viewport sequence — it's the fastest way to locate an invisible UI problem.
